title: Mass Exodus from the ICC: Chad Becomes Fifth Nation to Quit Amid US Pressure and Bias Claims
summary: The International Criminal Court, designed to prosecute humanity's worst offenses, is facing an unprecedented legitimacy crisis. Chad announced its withdrawal on Monday, becoming the fifth nation in recent months to abandon the tribunal. The military government condemned the court's "limited" effectiveness and its disproportionate focus on Africa: of 13 investigations opened since 2002, nine target African states, while four in other regions have seen "no concrete progress." Chad joins Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger—all under military rule—which quit in September, accusing the ICC of selective justice. Venezuela followed suit last week, citing "bias." The exodus is fueled by mounting US pressure. Washington's long-standing antagonism toward the court escalated after the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in 2024. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently declared a campaign to "systematically disable" the ICC. Chad's statement revealed that a US deputy secretary of state had urged the government to reconsider its membership. The timing is also notable: former ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, who secured the Netanyahu warrant, was dismissed over misconduct allegations—a move his defense team calls "politicised." The ICC, established by the Rome Statute, relies on member states to enforce its warrants. Before this wave, only Burundi and the Philippines had withdrawn. Hungary announced its exit just before hosting Netanyahu in 2025. Supporters argue the court is vital for holding perpetrators accountable, especially when national systems fail. But the perception of bias, amplified by US hostility, threatens to unravel a cornerstone of post-World War II justice. As one diplomat noted, "If the court is seen as a tool of powerful nations, it loses its moral authority."
why_it_matters: The ICC was designed to make sure no leader, no matter how powerful, can escape accountability for the worst crimes – but if countries walk away and powerful states undermine it, young people inherit a world where victims of atrocities may never see justice.

background_read: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is a permanent court in The Hague, Netherlands, set up in 2002 to try individuals for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity when national courts cannot or will not act.

The United States has never joined the ICC and has long opposed its authority, fearing American soldiers or officials could be prosecuted – a concern that intensified after the court sought to arrest Israeli leaders.
Several African nations, including Burundi in 2017, previously left the court, arguing it unfairly targets African leaders while ignoring abuses by powerful Western states.
The Rome Statute, the 1998 treaty that created the ICC, relies on member countries to enforce arrest warrants, which gives political pushback a major impact on the court's effectiveness.

perspectives.description: The court fills a gap when national legal systems are broken or unwilling to try their own leaders. Keeping the ICC strong deters future war criminals and gives a voice to victims everywhere.

The ICC has repeatedly been accused of focusing almost exclusively on Africa, ignoring powerful nations that commit similar acts. This perceived bias, along with international pressure, makes it look like a political weapon rather than a fair court.

The wave of withdrawals follows a historical pattern: the US never ratified the Rome Statute, and Russia and China also stay outside. Because the ICC relies entirely on members to arrest suspects, political support is fatal to its mandate. The more countries leave, the more the court becomes a symbol without real power.

If the pattern continues, the ICC may shrink to a core of European and a few other loyal states, leaving it unable to investigate conflicts elsewhere. Alternatively, the crisis could force serious reforms to address bias concerns and bring back former members. The outcome affects whether international law can ever truly bind the powerful.
